summaries.summary: Keyphrase generation predicts keyphrases from source text, requiring models to distill high-level information and locate specific important snippets.
Keyphrases may be present or absent, and keyphrase generation is set generation with variable set size and phrase token size.
Prior studies formulate keyphrase generation as Seq2Seq, using beam search over-generation and evaluating a fixed number of top predicted phrases, typically 5 or 10.
Beam search lacks dynamic keyphrase-number determination and phrase inter-relation modeling, reducing output diversity despite training-time diversity efforts.

Fixed-number evaluation mismatches variable ground truth keyphrases; dataset averages range from 5.3 to 15.7, variances reach 64.6, and KP20k oracle F1 score is 0.858 for INLINEFORM1 and 0.626 for INLINEFORM2.
The authors propose novel decoding strategies and evaluation metrics for keyphrase generation and list the work's main contributions.

Traditional keyphrase extraction uses candidate identification and ranking, with methods including bagged decision trees, Multi-Layer Perceptron, Support Vector Machine, PageRank, sequence labeling, and Pointer Networks.
Extractive models fail on absent keyphrases; CopyRNN, CorrRNN, semi-supervised methods, and structure information improve generation, but none generate variable numbers of phrases.
Seq2Seq learning with soft attention is widely used in natural language generation, including summarization, question generation, sentence simplification, and paraphrase generation.
The encoder converts source text embeddings INLINEFORM2 into INLINEFORM3 real-valued vectors INLINEFORM4 using a bidirectional GRU BIBREF27.
Dropout BIBREF28 is applied to both INLINEFORM0 and INLINEFORM1 for regularization.
The decoder is a uni-directional GRU generating a new state INLINEFORM0 at each time-step INLINEFORM1 from word embedding INLINEFORM2 and recurrent state INLINEFORM3.
The initial state INLINEFORM0 derives from final encoder state INLINEFORM1 via a single-layer feed-forward neural net, with dropout on embeddings INLINEFORM3 and GRU states INLINEFORM4.
An attention mechanism BIBREF18 infers importance INLINEFORM1 of each source word INLINEFORM2 using a 2-layer FNN energy function.
Outputs over all decoding steps INLINEFORM0 define a distribution over the source sequence.
Attention scores weight source encodings, which are concatenated with decoder state INLINEFORM0 to derive generative distribution INLINEFORM1.
The output size of INLINEFORM0 equals the target vocabulary size, and subscript INLINEFORM1 marks the abstractive nature of INLINEFORM2.
Pointer softmax BIBREF19 uses scalar switch INLINEFORM1 to interpolate abstractive distribution INLINEFORM2 and extractive distribution INLINEFORM3.
INLINEFORM0 is conditioned on attention-weighted source representation INLINEFORM1 and decoder state INLINEFORM2.
The objective is to generate a variable number of multi-word phrases using Seq2Seq with attention and pointer softmax mechanisms in the decoder.
One2Many examples can be divided into One2One examples, producing models like CopyRNN that generate one phrase and rely on beam search for more unique phrases.
One2Seq concatenates multiple phrases into a single sequence with delimiter INLINEFORM0 SEP INLINEFORM1 as the training target for sequence generation.
Notations define input text tokens, token embeddings, hidden states, output text tokens, time-steps, encoder or decoder subscripts, transformations, and concatenation.
Multiple keyphrases represent different text aspects, so diversity is desired, but over-generation with beam search is prone to similar phrases.
Delimiter-separated sequences cause identical tokens after delimiters due to homogeneous decoder states INLINEFORM2, motivating two plug-in components.
Semantic coverage introduces a uni-directional target encoder INLINEFORM0 encoding decoder-generated tokens INLINEFORM1 into hidden states INLINEFORM3 as extra decoder GRU input.
The target encoder is trained self-supervised by maximizing mutual information between phrase representations and source encoder final state INLINEFORM2 using classification loss.
INLINEFORM0 is bi-linear transformation.
Semantic coverage constrains generated keyphrase representations to be semantically close to source meaning and may guide generation.
Orthogonal regularization encourages delimiter-generating decoder states to differ by stacking them into matrix INLINEFORM0 and applying an orthogonal regularization loss.
The loss prefers orthogonality among hidden states INLINEFORM8 and improves diversity in tokens following delimiters.
The model adopts negative log-likelihood loss INLINEFORM0 and combines it into an overall loss.
INLINEFORM0 and INLINEFORM1 are hyper-parameters.
Exhaustive Decoding and Self-terminating Decoding differ in whether a model controls the number of phrases to output.
Fixed top-ranked evaluation requires beam search over-generation, with beam sizes 150 and 200 in BIBREF3 and BIBREF0, and One2Seq needs additional processes.
Beam search time complexity is INLINEFORM0, making exhaustive decoding expensive for One2Seq, where less than 5% of generated phrases are unique.
Self-terminating decoding generates a variable number of delimiter-joined phrases in one sequence and outputs INLINEFORM0 EOS INLINEFORM1 when adequate phrases are generated.

Self-terminating decoding conditions generation on previous phrases, models output dependency explicitly, and can decode more efficiently using greedy search or beam search on the top-scored sequence.
Precision, recall, and F INLINEFORM5 score are defined for top INLINEFORM3 predictions INLINEFORM4 against oracle set INLINEFORM2.
The number of generated keyphrases used for evaluation critically affects metrics, and three choices of INLINEFORM0 are compared.
A simple remedy sets INLINEFORM0 as a variable number specific to each data example and defines two new metrics.

F INLINEFORM1 @ INLINEFORM2 and F INLINEFORM3 @ INLINEFORM4 reflect variable phrase numbers, allow maximum INLINEFORM5 score of INLINEFORM6 only for exact phrase matches, and F INLINEFORM7 @ INLINEFORM8 is independent from model outputs.

Experiments report results on multiple datasets, with INLINEFORM0 denoting the delimiter-concatenated sequence-to-sequences model and INLINEFORM1 the model augmented with orthogonal regularization and semantic coverage.
Target sequences sort ground truth keyphrases by first occurrence in source text and append absent keyphrases to the end.
Baselines include four non-neural extractive models, CopyRNN, CopyRNN*, KEA, and Maui, with KEA and Maui trained on 50,000 documents from KP20k or StackEx.
Self-terminating decoding results are reported only for proposed models because no existing model supports such decoding strategy.
Scientific publication datasets include KP20k, Inspec, Krapivin, NUS, and SemEval; KP20k comprises more than half a million publications and uses abstracts, titles, and author keywords.
KP20k present-keyphrase results report INLINEFORM0 and INLINEFORM1 scores, and F INLINEFORM2 @ INLINEFORM3 shows consistent ranking with INLINEFORM4 for most cases.
Neural-based models outperform non-neural models by large margins, and implemented CopyRNN achieves better or comparable performance, especially on NUS and SemEval.

INLINEFORM0 and INLINEFORM1 yield comparable results to CopyRNN, INLINEFORM2 outperforms INLINEFORM3 on all metrics, and INLINEFORM5 outperforms One2One baselines on F INLINEFORM4 @10 for KP20k and Krapivin.
Inspired by the StackLite tag recommendation task on Kaggle, the authors build a StackExchange benchmark using question titles as source and user-assigned tags as target keyphrases.
StackEx has fewer keyphrases per data point and more general terminology such as Linux and Java, challenging models to distill major topics rather than select specific snippets.
Table TABREF37 reports StackEx performance, where INLINEFORM0 performs best and outperforms INLINEFORM1 by a large margin on absent-keyphrase generation tasks.

Experiments on KP20k and StackEx present keyphrase generation tasks in Table TABREF39 study predicting keyphrase number using self-terminating decoding and F INLINEFORM0 @ INLINEFORM1 and F INLINEFORM2 @ INLINEFORM3.
These experiments use beam search with only the top ranked prediction sequence as output, compare greedy search, and report only INLINEFORM0 and INLINEFORM1 for variable number generation.

Table TABREF39 shows greedy search consistently outperforms beam search, possibly because beam search generates short similar sequences, while lower F INLINEFORM0 @ INLINEFORM1 scores suggest over-generation may benefit recall.
Table TABREF44 shows semantic coverage significantly boosts INLINEFORM1 on all datasets, orthogonal regularization alone hurts INLINEFORM2, and INLINEFORM3 outperforms INLINEFORM4 on all datasets.
The authors use one quantitative and one qualitative metric to verify that target encoding and orthogonal regularization boost diversity of generated sequences.

Average unique predictions are 20.38 and 89.70 for INLINEFORM2 and INLINEFORM3, and t-SNE BIBREF35 on 2000 KP20k validation decoder hidden states shows INLINEFORM6 clusters more easily than INLINEFORM7.
A KP20k validation example with 29 ground truth phrases shows INLINEFORM0 predictions all start with “test”, while INLINEFORM1 predictions are diverse.

The paper proposes a recurrent generative model with two diversity-enhancing modules, new metrics, competitive performance on keyphrase generation datasets, and future work on target phrase order and order invariant set generation.

Generating absent keyphrases on scientific publication datasets is challenging, and existing studies often measure recall on tens or hundreds of keyphrases from exhaustive decoding with a large beam size while ignoring precision.
Table TABREF48 reports models' R@10/50 scores on the absent portion of five scientific paper datasets to align with previous studies.
CopyRNN with beam size of 200 suits absent keyphrase prediction, while INLINEFORM0 performs comparably with exhaustive decoding and diverse mechanisms and generally works better for top predictions.
Implementation uses 100-dimensional random word embeddings, 150 hidden units in encoder and decoder GRU, 150 hidden units in target encoder GRU, and vocabulary size 50,000.

Negative sampling randomly samples 16 samples from the same batch, making target encoding loss in Equation EQREF23 a 17-way classification loss; INLINEFORM0 sets INLINEFORM1 and INLINEFORM2 in Equation EQREF27 to 0.3, with dropout rate 0.1.
Optimization uses Adam BIBREF36 with learning rate INLINEFORM0, and the model is implemented using PyTorch BIBREF38 and OpenNMT BIBREF37.
Exhaustive decoding uses a beam size of 50 and a maximum sequence length of 40.
Following BIBREF0, lowercase and stemming are performed on both ground truth and generated keyphrases during evaluation.
The authors leave out 2,000 data examples as validation set for both KP20k and StackEx and report scores from checkpoints with best F INLINEFORM0 @ INLINEFORM1 validation performance.
